This is the one general judgment of all people at the single return of Christ, followed immediately by the eternal state. There is no room for an intervening millennium, since the righteous go straight into eternal life and the wicked into eternal punishment.
The scene reveals that how people treat Christ's needy brothers and sisters is how they treat Christ, a truth that shapes life in every age and will be made public at the end.

The Son of Man on his throne is Christ revealed in glory, and the separation exposes whether people have received the life of Christ that shows itself in love for the least. Union with him, not performance, is what the sheep did not even notice they possessed.

evidence.title: Universal judgment and eternal destinies
evidence.text: The judgment of “all the nations” issuing in eternal life and eternal punishment (25:46) mirrors Daniel 12:2 and John 5:28–29, which most interpreters, including partial preterists, read as the final resurrection and judgment.

evidence.title: Who are “the least of these”?
evidence.text: Some read “my brothers” as Christ's disciples or missionaries (compare 10:40–42; 12:48–50), others as any needy person; dispensationalists add the Jewish remnant. The identification affects whether the passage is about mission, compassion or Israel.

units.keyIssue: Whether this is the general final judgment, a judgment of the living nations before a millennium, or a covenantal judgment in AD 70.

related.title: Before the Son of Man comes: the towns of Israel
related.text: Sending out the Twelve, Jesus warns that they will be persecuted and says: “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next, for truly I say to you, you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.” The saying sits in a mission discourse that also predicts councils, floggings and governors (10:17–18), language that reappears in the Olivet Discourse. Albert Schweitzer famously thought it showed Jesus expected the end during that first mission and was mistaken, which makes the verse a test case for every view.

readings.reading: The disciples' mission to Israel would not be complete before the Son of Man came in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70. The persecutions of 10:17–23 match those of Matthew 24:9–13, and the coming is the same Daniel 7 coming in judgment and vindication.
The verse sets a firm limit on the parousia within the lifetime of the Twelve, and full preterists use it to argue that the one and only Second Coming happened in AD 70.

Many dispensationalists see the latter part of Matthew 10 as reaching beyond the first mission to the witness of Jewish believers in the future tribulation, which will not be finished before Christ returns; the mission to Israel was interrupted by the church age.
Interpretations include the resurrection, Pentecost, AD 70 or the final coming; many amillennialists take it as AD 70 or as a statement that the mission to Israel will continue until the end.
Some historic premillennialists read the verse as a prophetic telescoping of the near mission and the ongoing mission to Israel, which will remain unfinished until Christ's return.

related.title: Some standing here will not taste death
related.text: Jesus says the Son of Man will come with his angels in his Father's glory and repay each person according to what he has done, and that some standing there will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. Mark 9:1 has “until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power”, and Luke 9:27 simply “until they see the kingdom of God”. In all three Gospels the next scene is the transfiguration, six or eight days later.

readings.reading: Some of Jesus' hearers would live to see his coming in kingdom power, which partial preterists identify with the AD 70 judgment, about forty years later, when most but not all of the apostles had died. Verse 27 may describe the final judgment while verse 28 describes the near coming, or both may refer to AD 70.
The two verses describe one coming, with judgment and reward, within the lifetime of some present; therefore the final coming and judgment happened in AD 70.
The promise was fulfilled a week later in the transfiguration, when Peter, James and John saw a preview of Christ's kingdom glory, as 2 Peter 1:16–18 explains.
Many amillennialists see the fulfilment in the resurrection, ascension and Pentecost, when the kingdom came with power, or in the transfiguration as a foretaste.
Ladd and others see the kingdom coming in power in the resurrection and the outpouring of the Spirit, the present dimension of the kingdom that anticipates its future consummation.

related.title: All this will come upon this generation; your house is left desolate
related.text: Jesus pronounces the last of his woes on the scribes and Pharisees, saying they will fill up the measure of their fathers and that all the righteous blood shed from Abel to Zechariah will come upon “this generation” (23:35–36). He then laments over Jerusalem, “your house is left to you desolate”, and says they will not see him again until they say “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (23:37–39). The passage leads directly into the Olivet Discourse.

readings.reading: This is the key that unlocks the discourse. Judgment on “this generation” and the desolation of the “house” (the temple) are exactly what the disciples ask about in 24:1–3, and what was fulfilled in AD 70. Since “this generation” in 23:36 plainly means Jesus' contemporaries, it should mean the same in 24:34.
The judgment of 23:36, the desolation of 23:38 and the coming of 24:30 are one AD 70 event; full preterists see this as confirming that the parousia belongs to that generation.

Dispensationalists agree that 23:36 refers to the judgment of AD 70 but argue that 23:39 (“until you say, Blessed is he”) anticipates Israel's future repentance and welcome of the Messiah at the Second Coming (Zechariah 12:10; Romans 11:26).

The passage announces the end of the temple order in the judgment of AD 70; the “until” of 23:39 may point to a future turning of Jews to Christ or simply to their acknowledgment of him at the judgment.
Postmillennialists stress both the AD 70 judgment and the hope in 23:39, which many link with Romans 11 and expect to be fulfilled in a large-scale conversion of the Jewish people before the end.

related.title: You will see the Son of Man
related.text: At his trial, put under oath by the high priest Caiaphas, Jesus says: “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.” He combines Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13 and addresses the high priest and council in the plural. Mark 14:62 lacks “from now on”; Luke 22:69 says “from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God”.

readings.reading: “From now on” shows that the enthronement and coming begin with Jesus' death and resurrection and are publicly displayed in his judgment on the temple. The very leaders who condemned him would “see”, that is, recognise, his vindication within their lifetime. This strongly supports reading 24:30 as AD 70.
The high priest and council would see the coming, so it must have happened within their lifetime; full preterists treat this as one of their strongest texts.

Jesus warns his judges that they will one day see him as glorified judge, at his return or at the final resurrection when all stand before him; “seeing” may be in the future resurrection state, not within their earthly lifetime.
Many amillennialists see a progressive fulfilment: from the resurrection onward Christ reigns at God's right hand, and his judges will see him coming at the final judgment.
The exaltation began at once, but the coming on the clouds is the future return, at which the council members, raised for judgment, will see him.

related.title: The kingdom in your midst and the day of the Son of Man
related.text: Asked by Pharisees when the kingdom would come, Jesus says it does not come with signs to be observed, “for the kingdom of God is in your midst” (or “within you”). To the disciples he then speaks of “the day of the Son of Man”, like lightning, like the days of Noah and Lot, when one will be taken and another left, and anyone on the housetop must not go down for his goods. Asked “Where, Lord?”, he answers, “Where the corpse is, there the vultures (or eagles) will gather.”

readings.reading: Luke places sayings Matthew uses in 24:17–18, 27–28 and 37–41 together in one context with flight from the housetop and remembering Lot's wife, which suggests that a single historical crisis, the Roman judgment, is in view. Some partial preterists therefore apply Matthew 24:37–41 to AD 70 as well; others see Luke as combining two horizons.
Luke 17 describes the Second Coming at the end of the tribulation, when the judgment falls suddenly; those taken are removed in judgment (17:37), and those left enter the kingdom.
The present kingdom (17:21) and the future day (17:24) stand side by side: the kingdom is already here in Jesus, but its public manifestation awaits his return.
Ladd built much of his theology on texts like this one: the kingdom is present in Jesus' person and works, yet its consummation comes on a future day of the Son of Man.
The kingdom is not found by watching outward signs but is present where Christ is; the day of the Son of Man reveals what was within all along, and Lot's wife warns against clinging to the old life.

related.title: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem
related.text: As he approached the city on Palm Sunday, Jesus wept over it, saying that its enemies would set up a barricade (charax) around it, surround it, hem it in on every side, and dash it and its children to the ground, leaving not one stone upon another, “because you did not know the time of your visitation”. The prediction is concrete and local, describing the methods of a Roman siege.

readings.reading: This is an unmistakable prophecy of AD 70, fulfilled in detail when Titus built a siege wall around Jerusalem in three days and then destroyed the city. It shows that Jesus did speak specifically about the Roman siege and frames the Olivet Discourse as primarily about that event.
Dispensationalists agree this predicts AD 70 and see it as the consequence of Israel's rejection of the Messiah, which led to the postponement of the kingdom until the future.

The prediction shows the judgment of AD 70 as the covenant consequence of Israel's failure to recognise its visitation in Jesus, and it is widely agreed among amillennialists that it was fulfilled then.
The siege prophecy was fulfilled in AD 70, but historic premillennialists see it as the near judgment that, like Old Testament judgments, anticipates the far one.
Jesus weeps over a people who missed the day of their visitation because they looked for a different messiah. The warning applies whenever people cling to outward religion and miss Christ himself.

related.title: Jerusalem surrounded by armies; the times of the Gentiles
related.text: In Luke's version of the discourse, Jesus says: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near.” Those in Judea are to flee, because these are days of vengeance to fulfil all that is written. People will fall by the sword and be led captive among all nations, “and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.”

readings.reading: Luke's plain wording interprets the abomination of Matthew and Mark as the Roman armies around Jerusalem, a sign the disciples saw when Cestius Gallus advanced in AD 66. The “days of vengeance” are covenant judgment; partial preterists differ on whether the times of the Gentiles end in AD 70 or extend through history.

Luke 21:20–24 refers to AD 70, but the times of the Gentiles, which began with Nebuchadnezzar, continue until Christ returns to restore Jerusalem. That “until” shows Jerusalem's future, and it places the coming of 21:25–28 after a long interval.
The verse shows a long Gentile period between the fall of Jerusalem and the return of Christ, which historic premillennialists take as clear evidence that the discourse spans both events.
Luke separates AD 70 from the end by the times of the Gentiles, the present church age; Christ returns at its close.

Historicists have long linked the times of the Gentiles with the prophetic periods of Daniel and Revelation (the 1260 days or 42 months of Revelation 11:2), calculating them on the year-day principle.
The times of the Gentiles are the age of the gospel among the nations, which, following Romans 11:25–26, many postmillennialists expect to be followed by a large ingathering of Israel.

related.title: Daughters of Jerusalem, weep for yourselves
related.text: On the road to the cross Jesus turns to the women mourning for him: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.” Days are coming when people will say “Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore”, and will call on the mountains to fall on them and the hills to cover them (Hosea 10:8). “If they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?”

readings.reading: The prophecy was fulfilled within the lifetime of those women's children, in the siege of AD 70, when famine was so severe that a mother ate her own child, as Josephus records. The call to the mountains to cover them is echoed in Revelation 6:16, which partial preterists also apply to that judgment.
The words primarily anticipate AD 70, but the use of Hosea 10:8 in Revelation 6:16 shows they also foreshadow the final terror of the tribulation.
The saying applies to AD 70 and, by extension, to all who reject Christ and face judgment, as Revelation 6:16 shows in its picture of the final day.
The near fulfilment in AD 70 is clear; the wider principle of green and dry wood points to the greater judgment to come.

related.title: If I want him to remain until I come
related.text: When Peter asks what will happen to the beloved disciple, Jesus answers, “If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you?” The narrator then corrects a rumour that this disciple would not die, pointing out that Jesus did not say so, only “if it is my will”. Many date John's Gospel after AD 70, so the comment may reflect the disciple's old age or death.

readings.reading: Jesus hints that John might live until his coming in judgment in AD 70, which tradition says he did, living into the reign of Trajan. The narrator's correction warns against turning a conditional statement into a promise that John would see the final coming.
The verse shows that the apostles expected the coming within John's lifetime, and full preterists argue it was fulfilled in AD 70.
The saying is hypothetical: Jesus told Peter to follow him and not to speculate. The narrator's correction shows that the early church did not take it as a promise of an early return.
The point is about discipleship, not chronology: each disciple has his own calling, and the timing of Christ's return belongs to his will.

generation.text: The Greek word genea (Matthew 24:34; Mark 13:30; Luke 21:32) comes from a root meaning to be born. In the Greek Old Testament and the New Testament its main sense is the people living at one time, the contemporaries of someone, and by extension the span of a generation (around thirty to forty years); it can also mean descent or lineage (Matthew 1:17, where it means the generations in a family line), and in some contexts a kind or class of people sharing a character, as in Psalm 12:7 (LXX 11:8) or “a crooked and twisted generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5; Philippians 2:15). Standard lexicons such as BDAG give “those born at the same time, contemporaries” as a primary sense, and most commentators place Matthew 24:34 under it, though other proposals have long been made. In Matthew the phrase “this generation” (hē genea hautē) appears in 11:16, 12:41, 12:42, 12:45, 23:36 and 24:34, and related expressions (“evil and adulterous generation”, “faithless and twisted generation”) in 12:39, 16:4 and 17:17. In each case outside chapter 24 the reference is to the people of Jesus' own day, usually with a moral charge of unbelief. Three alternatives have been proposed for 24:34. First, “race” or “nation” (genos), meaning the Jewish people would survive until the end (Scofield, some earlier commentators); critics reply that genea and genos are different words and that this reading drains the saying of any time element. Second, “kind” or “type”, meaning faithless people would persist until the end (some patristic writers, and some amillennialists), which draws on the moral overtones of the word. Third, “the generation that sees these signs”, a future generation (Walvoord, Ice), arguing that the demonstrative “this” refers to the generation just described as seeing “all these things” (24:33). Preterists respond that “this” (hautē) in the Gospels normally points to what is near at hand, that Jesus uses “that” (ekeinē) when speaking of a future day (24:36), and that Matthew 23:36 sets the pattern. Others again accept “contemporaries” but limit “all these things” to the signs preceding the end rather than the coming itself (Blomberg, some amillennialists). The question is central, because if genea means Jesus' contemporaries and “all these things” includes 24:30, the coming of the Son of Man described there belongs to the first century.

uses.text: “To what shall I compare this generation?” Jesus compares his contemporaries to sulking children who rejected both John and himself; plainly the people of that time.

An “evil and adulterous generation” seeks a sign; the men of Nineveh and the queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with “this generation” and condemn it; the unclean spirit returns, “so also will it be with this evil generation”. All refer to Jesus' hearers.
“An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” Spoken to Pharisees and Sadducees present.
“O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you?” Addressed to the crowd and disciples who failed to heal the boy; uses moral description of contemporaries.

“Truly I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation.” The same formula as 24:34 (“truly I say to you”, “all these things”, “this generation”), applied to the judgment on Jerusalem and the temple announced in 23:38.
“Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.” The disputed verse; the parallels are Mark 13:30 and Luke 21:32.
“So all the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen generations.” Here genea means the successive links in a family line, showing the word's range.
Peter urges his hearers to “save yourselves from this crooked generation”, using the word of his contemporaries in Jerusalem, about AD 30–33.

readings.reading: Genea means Jesus' contemporaries, as everywhere else in Matthew, and especially 23:36, which uses the identical formula for AD 70. All the signs and the coming of 24:4–34 were fulfilled within forty years. The final coming of 24:36–25:46 is not covered by the time statement.
Genea means contemporaries, and since the whole discourse, including the parousia and the end of the age, is included in “all these things”, everything was fulfilled by AD 70.

The generation is the one that sees the signs of the future tribulation (24:33): those who see its beginning will see its end. An older dispensational alternative takes genea as the Jewish race, preserved until the end. Both readings protect the visible future coming of 24:30.

Genea means contemporaries, but “all these things” refers to the preliminary signs of 24:4–28, which were fulfilled within that generation, so the coming of 24:30 was “near” from then on and could not be dated.

Most amillennialists take genea as Jesus' contemporaries and see AD 70 as the fulfilment of the signs that also typify the end. Some take genea as a kind of people, unbelieving humanity, which will persist until Christ returns.
Classical historicists generally took genea as contemporaries and the prophecy as fulfilled in AD 70, then looked to Daniel and Revelation for the history that followed.

fulfilments.prophecyText: Not one stone will be left here upon another that will not be thrown down.
fulfilments.event: Titus ordered the whole city and temple demolished, leaving only three towers and part of the western wall.
fulfilments.note: The temple platform's retaining walls survived; most scholars take Jesus' words as referring to the temple buildings, which were completely destroyed.

fulfilments.prophecyText: Your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side.
fulfilments.event: Titus' army built a wall of circumvallation about 39 furlongs long with thirteen garrison forts around Jerusalem in three days, cutting off escape and supplies.
fulfilments.note: Some critical scholars argue that Luke wrote after 70 and shaped the wording to fit; others note that the language echoes Old Testament siege descriptions (Isaiah 29:3; Ezekiel 4:2) and was predictable for any siege.

fulfilments.prophecyText: When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near.
fulfilments.event: Cestius Gallus, governor of Syria, besieged Jerusalem, then withdrew without apparent reason and was routed at Beth-horon; many leading citizens left the city afterwards.
fulfilments.note: Preterists see Cestius' withdrawal as the window for Christians to flee; others think Titus' siege in 70 is the event in view, when flight was no longer possible.

fulfilments.prophecyText: Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.
fulfilments.event: The Jerusalem church, warned by an oracle, left the city before the war and settled in Pella in Perea, east of the Jordan.
fulfilments.note: The historicity of the Pella flight is disputed (S. G. F. Brandon and Gerd Lüdemann doubted it; Craig Koester and others defend it), and Pella lies in lowland, not in the mountains.

fulfilments.prophecyText: When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place.
fulfilments.event: After the temple was burned, Roman soldiers brought their standards into the temple court, set them up opposite the eastern gate and sacrificed to them. Earlier the Zealots had occupied the temple and installed a high priest by lot.
fulfilments.note: Futurists argue that Daniel 9:27 and 2 Thessalonians 2:4 require a future personal Antichrist, and that the standards were set up after the temple was already burning, too late to serve as a signal to flee.

fulfilments.prophecyText: Many will come in my name... false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs.
fulfilments.event: Theudas, the Egyptian and others led crowds to the Jordan, the wilderness and the Mount of Olives promising miraculous signs of deliverance.
fulfilments.note: These figures are prophets promising deliverance rather than explicit claimants to be the Christ, so some scholars think the match is approximate; Acts' dating of Theudas is also disputed.

fulfilments.prophecyText: There will be famines and earthquakes in various places.
fulfilments.event: A severe famine struck Judea under Claudius; earthquakes destroyed Laodicea and damaged Pompeii.
fulfilments.note: Such events occur in every period, so futurists and amillennialists regard them as typical of the age rather than unique markers.

fulfilments.prophecyText: They will deliver you up to tribulation and put you to death, and you will be hated by all nations for my name's sake.
fulfilments.event: Nero blamed Christians for the fire of Rome and executed many in horrific ways; James the Lord's brother was stoned in Jerusalem.
fulfilments.note: Persecution has recurred throughout church history; the match shows fulfilment within the generation but not necessarily exhaustive fulfilment.

fulfilments.prophecyText: This gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations.
fulfilments.event: Paul writes that the gospel has gone to the ends of the oikoumenē and been proclaimed in all creation under heaven.
fulfilments.note: Disputed: futurists argue that Paul's language is hyperbolic or representative and that “all nations” (Mark 13:10) remains to be fulfilled.

fulfilments.prophecyText: Then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now.
fulfilments.event: Josephus says the miseries of all men from the beginning of the world fall short of those of the Jews in this war.
fulfilments.note: Futurists argue that later events such as the Holocaust exceeded AD 70 in scale; preterists reply that the uniqueness is covenantal.

fulfilments.prophecyText: You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends... many will betray one another and hate one another.
fulfilments.event: During the siege the factions of John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora and Eleazar fought each other inside the city, burned the grain stores and killed fellow citizens suspected of wanting to desert.
fulfilments.note: Luke's verse concerns persecution of disciples rather than Jewish civil strife, so the match is thematic rather than exact.

fulfilments.prophecyText: Blessed are the barren... Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing in those days.
fulfilments.event: In the famine a woman named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, killed and ate her infant son, an act Josephus says horrified even the rebels.
fulfilments.note: The account recalls the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:53–57; some suspect Josephus heightened it for literary effect.

fulfilments.prophecyText: They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations.
fulfilments.event: Josephus gives 1,100,000 dead and 97,000 taken captive; captives were sent to Egyptian mines, to provincial arenas and to be sold.
fulfilments.note: Modern historians consider Josephus' totals inflated; Tacitus gives 600,000 besieged. The scale is not in doubt.

fulfilments.prophecyText: The powers of the heavens will be shaken. Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man.
fulfilments.event: Portents before the war: a sword-shaped star and a comet, a light around the altar at night, the eastern gate opening by itself, chariots and armies seen in the clouds, and a voice in the temple saying “Let us depart from here”.
fulfilments.note: Strongly disputed: most preterists do not rest their case on these portents but on the prophetic idiom of cosmic language; futurists argue that neither portents nor metaphor match a visible coming of Christ.

fulfilments.prophecyText: Your house is left to you desolate.
fulfilments.event: The temple was burned on the tenth of the month Lous (Ab), the same day of the year on which Solomon's temple had been burned by the Babylonians.
fulfilments.note: Jewish tradition commemorates both destructions on the ninth of Ab (Tisha B'Av); Josephus' date is the tenth.

fulfilments.prophecyText: They will tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you.
fulfilments.event: Woe-cries of Jesus son of Ananus, who from AD 62 cried “a voice against Jerusalem and the holy house” until killed by a Roman stone during the siege.
fulfilments.note: This is not a fulfilment of a specific prophecy but a striking parallel: another Jesus, also beaten and brought before the procurator, foretold the city's fall in Jeremiah's words.

timeline.label: Olivet Discourse
timeline.text: Jesus predicts the temple's destruction and gives the discourse in Passion Week, shortly before the crucifixion (dated AD 30 or 33).

timeline.label: Stephen martyred; church scattered
timeline.text: Stephen's death is followed by persecution that scatters believers through Judea and Samaria (date approximate, c. 33–35).

timeline.label: Caligula's statue crisis
timeline.text: The emperor Gaius orders his statue set up in the temple; the governor Petronius delays, and Gaius is assassinated in January 41 before it is done.
timeline.source: Josephus, Antiquities 18.8.2–9; Philo, Embassy to Gaius; Tacitus, Histories 5.9

timeline.label: James son of Zebedee killed
timeline.text: Herod Agrippa I executes James and imprisons Peter, then dies at Caesarea; Judea returns to procurators.

timeline.label: Theudas
timeline.text: Under the procurator Fadus, Theudas leads a crowd to the Jordan promising to part it; he is beheaded (c. 44–46).

timeline.label: Famine in Judea
timeline.text: A severe famine under Claudius strikes Judea; Antioch's Christians send relief by Barnabas and Saul (c. 46–48).

timeline.label: Jews expelled from Rome
timeline.text: Claudius expels Jews from Rome after disturbances “at the instigation of Chrestus”, often taken as a reference to disputes over Christ.

timeline.label: The Egyptian on the Mount of Olives
timeline.text: Under Felix, an Egyptian prophet gathers followers on the Mount of Olives, promising that Jerusalem's walls will fall; Felix's troops scatter them (c. 54–58).

timeline.label: Laodicea earthquake
timeline.text: An earthquake destroys Laodicea in Asia, which rebuilds from its own resources.

timeline.label: James the Just stoned; Jesus son of Ananus
timeline.text: Between procurators, the high priest Ananus has James the Lord's brother stoned. At Tabernacles a peasant, Jesus son of Ananus, begins crying woe on Jerusalem and continues for seven years. An earthquake damages Pompeii (62 or 63).
timeline.source: Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1; Jewish War 6.5.3; Tacitus, Annals 15.22

timeline.label: Fire of Rome; Nero's persecution; temple complex finished
timeline.text: Nero blames Christians for the great fire and executes many. Around this time the work on the temple complex is completed under Albinus.

timeline.label: War begins; Cestius Gallus withdraws
timeline.text: Florus plunders the temple treasury; sacrifices for the emperor stop; Cestius Gallus besieges Jerusalem in the autumn, then withdraws and is defeated at Beth-horon.

timeline.label: Vespasian in Galilee
timeline.text: Vespasian and Titus reconquer Galilee; Jotapata falls and Josephus surrenders and predicts Vespasian's rise.

timeline.label: Zealots seize the temple; Nero dies
timeline.text: Zealots occupy the temple, appoint a high priest by lot and, with Idumean allies, kill the former high priests; Nero commits suicide in June.

timeline.label: Year of the four emperors
timeline.text: Galba, Otho and Vitellius rise and fall in civil war; Vespasian is proclaimed emperor in July and secures Rome by December.

timeline.label: Siege and fall of Jerusalem
timeline.text: Titus begins the siege at Passover, builds a wall around the city, burns the temple in late August, and takes the upper city in September.

timeline.label: Triumph in Rome
timeline.text: Vespasian and Titus celebrate a triumph displaying the temple's menorah and table, later carved on the Arch of Titus; the temple tax is redirected to Jupiter Capitolinus.

timeline.label: Fall of Masada
timeline.text: The last rebel stronghold falls after its defenders' mass suicide; the date is debated between 73 and 74.
